title: MCI — Exam 2 (Mass Casualty Incident Management)
description: Integrated scenario-style exam spanning all 14 MCI chapters: disaster types, METHANE, ICS and officer roles, scene layout, START/JumpSTART/SALT triage, treatment and transport, CBRNE, blast/hostile events, special MCIs, and recovery.

questions.text: Which factor DEFINES whether an incident is an MCI?
options: Casualties exceed the resources immediately available
questions.explanation: An MCI is defined by the resource gap, not a fixed number. Local plans may use counts only as activation tiers.
questions.hint: Think capacity, not counts.

questions.text: A hurricane floods the county's only hospital and knocks out cell towers; victims are still being found days later. This is BEST classified as:
questions.explanation: Victims still appearing = open; damaged infrastructure = compound; the community needs outside help = uncompensated (a disaster).
questions.hint: Ask three questions: victims finite? infrastructure intact? can the system absorb it?

questions.text: Which injury pattern should you anticipate FIRST after a major earthquake in a dense city?
options: Entrapment with crush injury and crush syndrome
questions.explanation: Collapsed structures trap people; prolonged compression causes crush syndrome at release.
questions.hint: What does a collapsed building do to the people inside?

questions.text: Two days after an ice storm, several members of one family present with headache, nausea, and confusion. The MOST likely cause is:
options: Carbon monoxide from a generator or heater used indoors
questions.explanation: Post-storm CO poisoning from generators/heaters is a predictable 'second wave' killer. Remove everyone and give high-flow O2.
questions.hint: What do people use when the power is out?

questions.text: You are first on scene at a coach rollover with ~35 casualties. Your partner should:
options: Perform a rapid recon and global sort while you establish command and send METHANE
Start loading green patients into your ambulance
Begin CPR on the first pulseless patient
questions.explanation: First crew: one takes command/comms, the other recons and sorts. Nobody gets 'sucked in' to single-patient care.
questions.hint: First-in doesn't get sucked in.

questions.text: In a METHANE report, 'A' tells incoming units:
options: Access and egress routes and the rendezvous/staging point
questions.explanation: M-E-T-H-A-N-E: Major incident, Exact location, Type, Hazards, Access, Number of casualties, Emergency services.
questions.hint: How do incoming units get in safely?

questions.text: Which METHANE 'N' line is BEST?
options: 'Approximately 40: 6 red, 12 yellow, 22 green; at least 4 children.'
questions.explanation: Estimates with a severity split and special groups let resources and hospitals move now.
questions.hint: Numbers + severity + special groups.

questions.text: Arriving at a warehouse, you see 4 workers collapsed near a loading bay with no visible trauma and a faint acrid smell. Per Step 1-2-3 Plus you should:
options: Not approach; withdraw upwind, isolate, report (METHANE) and request HazMat
Enter with a BVM and oxygen
Wait for the workers to recover
Approach with caution and assess the nearest worker
questions.explanation: Three or more unexplained casualties = Step 3: do not approach. Plus: instruct people to get out, disrobe, and decontaminate.
questions.hint: How many are down, and is there an obvious cause?

questions.text: The correct order of CSCATTT priorities begins with:
questions.explanation: CSCA (management) must be in place before TTT (medical support) can work well.
questions.hint: Management before medicine.

questions.text: A person leading an ICS Branch is titled:
questions.explanation: Section = Chief, Branch = Director, Division/Group = Supervisor, Unit = Leader, Staging = Manager.
questions.hint: Chief → ? → Supervisor → Leader.

questions.text: Fire, police, and EMS all have jurisdiction at a stadium collapse. The ICS model that gives them ONE set of objectives while each keeps authority over its own resources is:
options: Single Command by the highest rank
questions.explanation: Unified Command co-locates agency commanders at one command post with one Incident Action Plan.
questions.hint: One incident, one plan, several agencies.

questions.text: The Medical Group Supervisor is directly managing 10 ambulance crews and 3 rescue teams. The correct ICS response is to:
options: Accept it — span of control doesn't apply in emergencies
Appoint unit leaders (triage, treatment, transport) and a staging manager to restore span of control
questions.explanation: Span of control is ~3–7 (≈5 optimal). Expand the organization when it's exceeded.
questions.hint: How many people can one supervisor manage well?

questions.text: Which is a General Staff (Section Chief) position?
questions.explanation: General Staff = Operations, Planning, Logistics, Finance/Admin. Safety, Liaison, and PIO are Command Staff.
questions.hint: Chiefs vs Officers.

questions.text: A senior EMS chief arrives at your incident. Command transfers when:
options: After a face-to-face briefing, the chief accepts, and the transfer is announced to all units
questions.explanation: Formal transfer of command: brief, accept, announce. Arrival or rank alone does not transfer command.
questions.hint: Brief — Accept — ?

questions.text: Who assigns destination hospitals and keeps the patient log at an MCI?
questions.explanation: Transport matches patients to hospitals by capability/capacity and logs tag #, unit, destination, time.
questions.hint: Who 'moves and tracks'?

questions.text: Fifteen minutes into an MCI, no updated casualty count has reached command. The triage officer is found performing an IO on a child. The BEST correction is:
options: Let the triage officer finish; children take priority
Stop all triage until the IO is placed
Reassign the triage officer to transport
Hand the child to the treatment team and return the triage officer to sorting and reporting counts
questions.explanation: Triage interventions are seconds-long only. When triage stops, untagged reds go unfound.
questions.hint: What is the triage officer's ONE job?

questions.text: Mutual-aid ambulances arriving at an MCI should:
options: Drive to the treatment area and load the nearest patient
Check in at staging and wait with their vehicle until called to the loading zone
questions.explanation: Staging keeps vehicles organized; Transport calls them forward. Self-dispatch breaks flow and tracking.
questions.hint: Check in, keys in, crews in.

questions.text: Dead victims at an MCI should generally be:
options: Placed in ambulances to protect them from weather
Transported first to clear the scene
Moved to the treatment area for documentation
Left in place unless they block access to the living; secured and screened from view
questions.explanation: Leave in place: saves resources and preserves evidence and identification. The morgue manager coordinates with police/ME.
questions.hint: Who needs the stretchers more?

questions.text: The treatment area is full, ambulances are idle at the loading zone, and nothing is leaving. The MOST likely failure point is:
options: The handoff between treatment and transport (prioritization/loading)
questions.explanation: Idle ambulances + full treatment area = treatment isn't releasing patients or transport isn't loading them.
questions.hint: Patients in, nobody out — where's the bottleneck?

questions.text: The decontamination corridor belongs in the:
questions.explanation: Warm = contamination reduction zone.
questions.hint: Between the hazard and the support area.

questions.text: Which treatment-area design is BEST?
options: Next to the helicopter landing zone
Upwind in the cold zone, red section nearest the loading zone exit, one-way flow
Downwind for ventilation with red in the center
Inside the warm zone for speed
questions.explanation: Safety plus flow: upwind, cold zone, reds exit first, one direction.
questions.hint: Who leaves first, and which way is the wind blowing?

questions.text: An unattended backpack is found 20 m from your casualty collection point after a bombing. You should:
options: Continue working — it's probably lost property
Carry the backpack away from patients
Move patients and staff out of line of sight beyond the stand-off distance and notify police
questions.explanation: Assume a secondary device. Pipe-bomb mandatory evacuation is ~70 ft (preferred outdoor ~1,200 ft).
questions.hint: Who is the second bomb for?

questions.text: Staging for ambulances should be:
options: Out of sight of the hazard, on the approach route, with one-way access to the loading zone
questions.explanation: Staging is remote, safe, organized, and released by Transport.
questions.hint: Safe, organized, and not in the way.

questions.text: START: a non-ambulatory adult has RR 34, radial pulse present, and follows commands. Category:
questions.explanation: RR > 30 = Immediate.
questions.hint: RPM: 30-2-Can do.

questions.text: START: RR 24, radial pulse present but capillary refill 4 seconds (warm day), follows commands. Category:
questions.explanation: CRT > 2 s = perfusion failure = Immediate.
questions.hint: Check the 'P' in RPM.

questions.text: START: RR 30, radial present, CRT 1 s, follows commands, can't walk. Category:
questions.explanation: The cut-off is RR MORE than 30. All other checks pass → Delayed.
questions.hint: Is 30 more than 30?

questions.text: JumpSTART: a 4-year-old is apneic after airway positioning but has a palpable pulse. You give 5 rescue breaths and she begins breathing. Category:
questions.explanation: Breathing after rescue breaths = Immediate. If still apneic after 5 breaths = Deceased.
questions.hint: What does breathing only after help mean?

questions.text: JumpSTART: a 6-year-old has RR 38, palpable peripheral pulse, is alert, and has a deformed femur. Category:
questions.explanation: JumpSTART's normal range is 15–45; pulse present and Alert → Delayed. (RR 38 would be red in adult START.)
questions.hint: Kids breathe faster — what's the JumpSTART range?

questions.text: JumpSTART: a 3-year-old has RR 26, palpable pulse, and responds to a painful stimulus only with rigid arm extension. Category:
questions.explanation: Inappropriate response to pain (posturing) or Unresponsive = Immediate.
questions.hint: Is that an 'appropriate P'?

questions.text: During a cold night-time MCI, the most reliable START perfusion check is:
questions.explanation: Cold and darkness make capillary refill unreliable.
questions.hint: Which sign does the cold distort?

questions.text: In SALT global sorting, which casualties are assessed FIRST?
options: Those who are still or have obvious life threats
Those who walk to the designated area
questions.explanation: Walk → last, Wave → second, Still/obvious life threat → first.
questions.hint: Who is most likely to need a lifesaving intervention?

questions.text: SALT: after a tourniquet stops arterial thigh bleeding, the patient obeys commands, has a peripheral pulse, and no respiratory distress. Category:
questions.explanation: After the LSI all four questions are YES; the injury is significant (not minor) → Delayed. Write TQ + time on the tag.
questions.hint: Re-ask the four questions AFTER the intervention.

questions.text: SALT, 70 casualties, 3 ambulances: a man with ~90% full-thickness burns is breathing shallowly and unresponsive. Category NOW:
options: Expectant — comfort care and re-triage when resources improve
questions.explanation: Expectant = alive but unlikely to survive given CURRENT resources. Re-triage as resources arrive.
questions.hint: Survival given what you have right now?

questions.text: A trauma system's over-triage rate rises sharply during an MCI. The expected effect is:
options: Higher mortality among the truly critical
questions.explanation: Over-triage floods red areas and transport, burying true reds (Frykberg).
questions.hint: What happens to the real reds?

questions.text: A triage tag should be attached to:
questions.explanation: Clothing gets cut off in treatment; tags on clothing get lost.
questions.hint: What gets removed in the treatment area?

questions.text: Which intervention BEST fits the MCI treatment area?
options: Second IV lines on stable greens
Full secondary survey on every yellow
questions.explanation: Do what changes near-term survival (MARCH); defer what slows flow.
questions.hint: MARCH starts with M.

questions.text: The nearest hospital to a bombing is usually overwhelmed early because:
options: It is always the trauma center
Less-injured victims self-present there before EMS patients arrive
questions.explanation: 'Upside-down triage': the walking wounded reach the closest ED first.
questions.hint: Who gets there first, and how?

questions.text: A hospital receives 25 casualties in the first hour after an explosion. Its approximate total expected is:
questions.explanation: CDC rule of thumb: roughly double the first-hour arrivals.
questions.hint: Rule of thumb: multiply by…

questions.text: Which loading plan is MOST efficient?
options: One red plus one or two greens per ambulance; greens in bulk by bus with a medic
Wait until all patients are treated
questions.explanation: Use every seat sensibly; move greens in bulk.
questions.hint: Fill the seats wisely.

questions.text: Hospital capacity during an MCI should be obtained through:
options: A single Medical Communications Coordinator / hospital coordination center
questions.explanation: One voice to hospitals prevents duplicate calls and skewed distribution.
questions.hint: How many voices should hospitals hear?

questions.text: In the ERG, which pages give initial isolation and protective action distances?
questions.explanation: Yellow = by ID number, Blue = by name, Orange = guides, Green = distances.
questions.hint: Gap = Green.

questions.text: NFPA 704: the RED quadrant represents:
questions.explanation: Blue health, red flammability, yellow instability, white special.
questions.hint: Red = fire.

questions.text: Which PPE level uses an air-purifying respirator and requires a known agent with adequate oxygen?
questions.explanation: Level C = APR/PAPR + splash suit; it filters ambient air but supplies no oxygen.
questions.hint: Filter vs supplied air.

questions.text: The single most effective first decontamination step is:
questions.explanation: Disrobing removes most external contamination (often quoted ~80–90%).
questions.hint: What is touching the skin most?

questions.text: A critically injured, contaminated patient with arterial bleeding reaches the decon line. Best action:
options: Tourniquet by protected staff during rapid gross decon, then transport
Wait at the end of the decon queue
questions.explanation: Combine LSIs with rapid decon. A contaminated ambulance and crew become casualties.
questions.hint: Never skip decon — but don't let them bleed out either.

questions.text: Subway riders have pinpoint pupils, copious secretions, wheezing, vomiting, and fasciculations. The antidote combination is:
options: Atropine plus pralidoxime (with a benzodiazepine for seizures)
questions.explanation: Cholinergic crisis = nerve agent → atropine + 2-PAM; benzo for seizures.
questions.hint: Wet + pinpoint + twitching.

questions.text: Atropine for nerve-agent poisoning is titrated to:
options: Dry bronchial secretions and easy breathing
questions.explanation: Tachycardia and persistent miosis are not reasons to stop or keep giving atropine.
questions.hint: What kills these patients?

questions.text: A nerve-agent casualty is seizing and apneic after decon. Using DuoDote/ATNAA kits, the correct dosing is:
options: 3 kits rapidly plus a benzodiazepine, with ventilatory support
questions.explanation: Severe = 3 kits + benzo. Repeat atropine until secretions dry.
questions.hint: Mild 1, severe…

questions.text: A house-fire victim is unresponsive with BP 70/40 and SpO2 reading 99%. Which antidote is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Smoke + shock → cyanide (and CO). Hydroxocobalamin is safe with CO; nitrites worsen oxygen delivery.
questions.hint: What else is in smoke besides CO?

questions.text: Workers exposed to a gas smelling of 'freshly cut hay' feel fine 30 minutes later. Best disposition:
options: Rest and observe ~24 h for delayed pulmonary edema
questions.explanation: Phosgene's latent period: pulmonary edema 2–24 h; exertion worsens it.
questions.hint: Some agents bite later.

questions.text: A theater audience collapses with pinpoint pupils, slow shallow respirations, dry skin, and no fasciculations. Treatment:
questions.explanation: Dry miosis + respiratory depression = opioid agent, not a nerve agent.
questions.hint: Wet or dry?

questions.text: Which Category A agent requires airborne PLUS contact precautions?
questions.explanation: Smallpox spreads by respiratory and contact routes; anthrax, botulism, and tularemia don't spread person-to-person.
questions.hint: Which one spreads between people through the air?

questions.text: An alert, afebrile adult has ptosis, double vision, slurred speech, and difficulty swallowing that is progressing downward. Suspect:
questions.explanation: Descending symmetric flaccid paralysis with a clear mind = botulism; prepare for respiratory failure.
questions.hint: Which way is the weakness travelling?

questions.text: A patient was irradiated by a hidden source but is not contaminated. The risk to EMS providers is:
options: None — the patient is not radioactive
questions.explanation: Exposure doesn't make a person radioactive; contamination is the transferable risk.
questions.hint: X-ray or mud?

questions.text: A dirty-bomb victim has a traumatic amputation with arterial bleeding and a radiation detector is alarming. Priority:
options: Tourniquet and trauma care now in standard PPE, then decon
questions.explanation: RDDs injure by blast; radiation contamination is rarely immediately life-threatening. Life threats first.
questions.hint: Bomb first, dirt second.

questions.text: Moving from 2 m to 4 m away from a radiation point source changes your dose rate to:
questions.explanation: Inverse-square law: double the distance → ¼ the dose rate.
questions.hint: Distance squared.

questions.text: The most common mechanism of injury in explosions is:
questions.explanation: Fragments injure the most people; primary blast is worse in enclosed spaces.
questions.hint: What flies through the air?

questions.text: A survivor of a bus bombing walked away with ruptured eardrums and mild dyspnea; SpO2 now 93%. Best action:
options: Needle decompression for all blast victims
Treat as possible blast lung: O2, monitor, transport for observation
questions.explanation: Enclosed blast + TM rupture + hypoxia = evolving blast lung risk; caution with fluids and positive pressure.
questions.hint: Enclosed space + ears + breathing.

questions.text: In TECC direct threat (hot zone), the recommended medical intervention is:
options: Tourniquet for life-threatening extremity hemorrhage and movement to cover
questions.explanation: Direct threat = cover + tourniquet only. Airway and other care wait for indirect threat.
questions.hint: Under fire, what's the one fix?

questions.text: A Rescue Task Force typically:
options: Enters cleared warm-zone areas with law-enforcement escort to stop bleeding and extract casualties
Works only in the cold zone
questions.explanation: RTF = EMS/fire in ballistic PPE + police escort in the warm zone → CCP.
questions.hint: Escorted, warm, fast.

questions.text: Hartford Consensus THREAT stands for:
options: Threat, Hazards, Rescue, Exposure, Access, Transport
Threat suppression, Hemorrhage control, Rapid Extrication, Assessment, Transport
Triage, Hospital, Radio, Evacuation, Airway, Treatment
Tourniquet, Hemostatics, Recovery, Extraction, Analgesia, Transfer
questions.explanation: THREAT puts hemorrhage control right after stopping the threat.
questions.hint: Stop the killing, stop the dying.

questions.text: A worker pinned under a slab for 5 hours is about to be freed. The MOST important preparation is:
options: IV normal saline before release with cardiac monitoring and hyperkalemia drugs ready
questions.explanation: Fluids before freedom; release can trigger fatal hyperkalemia. Avoid potassium-containing fluids.
questions.hint: What floods the circulation at release?

questions.text: Crowd-crush victims die mainly from:
questions.explanation: They cannot expand their chests. Relieve pressure, then ventilate.
questions.hint: What can't they do while squeezed?

questions.text: The first hazard control at a commuter-rail derailment is:
questions.explanation: Overhead lines and third rails kill rescuers.
questions.hint: What powers the train?

questions.text: Before terminating command, the MOST important check is:
options: Patient counts reconcile across tags, transport log, and hospital arrivals
All units have returned to quarters
questions.explanation: Tags = transport log = hospitals (+ dead + released). A mismatch means someone is missing.
questions.hint: Do the numbers add up?

questions.text: Which approach to responder mental health after an MCI is recommended?
options: Psychological First Aid with voluntary peer support and follow-up
Mandatory single-session group debriefing for all
questions.explanation: PFA (Look, Listen, Link) is recommended; forced single-session debriefing may harm.
questions.hint: Offer, don't force.
